science.headline: X-ray scans reveal famous 'early reptile' fossil was actually a water-dwelling animal
summary: A small fossil found in Scotland in 1984 was seen for almost thirty years as one of the earliest known reptiles. Nicknamed "Lizzie" and named Westlothiana lizziae, it is about 345 million years old. New research in Nature, led by scientists at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, now suggests it was a very different kind of animal.

The skeleton is preserved in two crushed slabs of rock, which made it hard to read. Researchers used powerful X-ray imaging at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, to look inside and rebuild hidden parts of the animal. They found a primitive skull, internal gills containing bone, and a fish-like mouth with thousands of tiny teeth. These features rule out a place in the family line leading to reptiles, and point to an aquatic or amphibious creature.
science.bigPicture: Lizzie had long served as a reference point for when and how amniotes first evolved, so reclassifying it affects how scientists picture that early history. The study suggests that land-style features built up gradually in animals that lived both in and out of the water. It may also affect how fossil footprints are interpreted. Some tracks once credited to early amniotes could instead have been left by older amphibious relatives, though that would need further study.
science.originalTitle: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades

science.headline: Giant deer bones hint people may have reached Ireland earlier than thought
summary: Researchers studying Ballynamintra Cave, near Dungarvan in County Waterford, found signs that hunter-gatherers may have been in southern Ireland about 13,500 years ago. That would be nearly a thousand years before the earliest firm evidence now accepted. The study was published on Nov. 26 in the Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy. It combines new digging at the cave with a fresh look at animal bones first collected there in 1878–1882 and kept at the National Museum of Ireland.

In that old collection, the team found two leg bones from the extinct giant deer that carry marks consistent with butchery of fresh bone. One upper foreleg bone has a flat chopping mark that fits a heavy stone blade used on the elbow joint, plus wolf gnaw marks. A lower hindleg bone has a possible impact mark and tiny cracks from splitting it open for marrow. Oxford radiocarbon dating put that bone at 13,573–13,321 years ago. The current earliest firm evidence in Ireland is a butchered brown bear bone from a County Clare cave, dated to roughly 12,800–12,600 years ago.
science.bigPicture: If people really were in Ireland 13,500 years ago, it would push back the known arrival of humans there and change how scientists picture early movement across northwest Europe at the end of the last Ice Age. The team also showed that undisturbed Ice Age layers still survive in the cave, which overturns the idea that 19th-century diggers emptied Ireland's bone caves. Further excavations are scheduled, and Ice Age deposits appear to continue into unexplored passages. Those digs could turn up stone tools or bone points that might confirm early settlement, though that remains a possibility rather than a result.
science.originalTitle: Giant deer bones may push human arrival in Ireland back by 1,000 years

science.headline: Northwestern physicists trap and cool a single positron, opening the way to a precise antimatter test
summary: Physicists at Northwestern University have gained a high level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter partner of the electron. The team captured a fast-moving positron released by radioactive decay of sodium-22, slowed it, and cooled it to about 0.3 degrees above absolute zero. They then held it in a near-perfect vacuum, using electric and magnetic fields to keep it suspended so it never touched the walls of its container. Contact with ordinary matter would destroy it.

The positron stayed in the trap for months and settled into its lowest quantum energy state. Using microwaves, the researchers moved it between energy levels and detected the changes, a setup they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." The study was led by Gerald Gabrielse, and Ph.D. student Thomas Myers is its first author.
science.bigPicture: The next step is to measure the positron's magnetic properties as precisely as the team earlier measured the electron's, to about one part in 10 trillion, and then compare the two. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that electrons and positrons should be nearly perfect mirror images. Any unexpected difference could point to a gap in that theory. It might also offer clues to why the universe holds so much more matter than antimatter. Whether such a difference exists is still unknown, and the measurement itself has yet to be made.
science.originalTitle: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

science.headline: Physicists find Einstein's Brownian motion model falls short for near-light-speed particles in early-universe plasma
summary: Physicists at MIT and UC Santa Barbara have found that a well-known idea from Einstein misses something when particles move close to the speed of light. In 1905, Einstein explained that a particle in a fluid is slowed by drag while also being jostled by countless random pushes from surrounding atoms and molecules. The new work looked at heavy quarks moving through quark-gluon plasma, the extremely hot mixture of particles that filled the universe just after the Big Bang.

The researchers calculated the forces on a heavy quark in a simple model: a gas of quarks and gluons that interact only weakly. For small changes in motion, the results matched the familiar bell-shaped pattern. For larger changes, though, the pattern was lopsided. Big jolts happened more often than the traditional model predicts, and large slowdowns were more likely than equally large speed-ups. The study was published in Physical Review Letters.
science.bigPicture: Scientists can briefly create tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma in particle accelerators, and heavy quarks moving through them can reveal details about the plasma's inner structure. The new calculations suggest that how often rare, large jolts occur may depend on the plasma's microscopic nature, which could offer a new kind of clue. If the predictions are compared with accelerator results, physicists may learn more about this ancient state of matter and the conditions soon after the Big Bang. That remains a possibility for future work, and the researchers describe it as something their calculations could help with, not something already shown.
science.originalTitle: Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

science.headline: Underwater Robots Help Identify First Salp Species Living Only in the Deep Sea
summary: Researchers have formally described a new species called the glass salp, Vitreosalpa gemini. It is the first salp known to live only in the deep sea. Salps are barrel-shaped, jellylike animals that drift through the ocean. Scientists count 50 known species, and most of them live offshore near the surface.

The first sighting of this unfamiliar salp in Monterey Bay's deep water came more than 20 years ago. Larry Madin then used specimens and data gathered by MBARI's remotely operated vehicles to write the description, which appeared in the journal Marine Biodiversity. The glass salp lives at depths of 280 to 2,200 meters (920 to 7,200 feet). It is a slow swimmer with a delicate, watery body. Its feeding and metabolic rates are much lower than those of its surface-dwelling relatives. Without sunlight, it eats detritus and single-celled protozoans rather than living phytoplankton.
science.bigPicture: Salps are an important link in the ocean carbon cycle, because they eat phytoplankton and tiny bits of organic material called marine snow. Their blooms can move carbon quickly to the deep seafloor. Finding a salp that lives only in the deep sea shows how much remains unknown in the largest living space on the planet, as Madin put it. Robotic vehicles that can observe fragile animals undisturbed may help scientists learn more about other gelatinous creatures in the deep ocean.
science.originalTitle: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea

science.headline: Researcher Proposes Calling Mitochondria the 'Lungs of the Cell' to Help Students Learn
summary: Many people learn that mitochondria are the "powerhouse of the cell," a phrase that goes back to a 1957 Scientific American article. Dr. Aaron Morton, a regenerative medicine researcher at Texas A&M University, thinks this description can leave students with a fact they memorize but cannot use. He has met students, even graduate students, who can explain how oxygen gets into the lungs and bloodstream but not what happens once it reaches cells.

Morton suggests a second description: mitochondria are the "lungs of the cell." He introduced the phrase in a recently published study about a new way to examine mitochondrial structure. His reasoning is that mitochondria use oxygen, much as lungs do, so the comparison ties breathing to what happens inside cells.
science.bigPicture: Morton does not want teachers to drop the "powerhouse" idea. He sees the two phrases working together: "powerhouse" says what mitochondria help produce, and "lungs of the cell" helps explain how and why oxygen matters. He hopes teachers in high school biology and introductory college courses will try the comparison without waiting for textbooks to change. The summary of the article notes that how well this metaphor works as a teaching tool has not yet been established, so it remains an idea to test in classrooms.
science.originalTitle: Mitochondria rebranding: Goodbye, powerhouse of the cell. Hello, lungs of the cell?

science.headline: Ordinary-Looking Metal EuSi Shows Rare, Hidden Form of Magnetism
summary: Researchers have found strong evidence of an unusual magnetic state in europium silicide (EuSi), a fairly simple metallic compound. The material has no overall magnetization, yet its magnetism strongly affects how its electrons behave. The state is called p-wave magnetism, and in it an electron's spin is tied to the direction it travels. The work began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids in Dresden, Germany, where Dr. Erjian Cheng grew high-quality single crystals of the material.

Between roughly 33 and 62 kelvin (about minus 400 to minus 348 degrees Fahrenheit), the magnetic moments of the europium atoms arrange themselves in a repeating spiral. Their orientations balance out across the spiral, so the material shows no net magnetization. A team of 38 scientists from 19 institutions confirmed the spiral using neutron diffraction. Photoemission measurements then showed magnetic energy separations above 100 millielectronvolts, and spin-resolved measurements showed the electron spin polarization changing sign across successive magnetic zones. The spiral can also twist in two opposite directions, forming domains of opposite handedness about ten micrometers across, and these domains responded differently to circularly polarized light.
science.bigPicture: Because EuSi is a relatively simple metal, it may give scientists a practical way to study p-wave magnetism in detail. That could help researchers better understand exotic quantum materials. The researchers say the field could eventually lead to new ways of controlling electronic properties, and possibly to future electronic technologies. Those applications are still possibilities, and this work mainly offers a clearer view of the underlying physics.
science.originalTitle: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism

science.headline: Pollen in a 2,200-year-old Roman ship's coatings reveals its waterproofing recipes and repairs
summary: Researchers studied the protective coatings on Ilovik-Paržine 1, a Roman Republic ship that sank about 2,200 years ago off the coast of what is now Croatia. Of 10 coating samples, most were pitch made from pine. One sample combined pine tar with beeswax, a mixture Greek shipbuilders called zopissa. The beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to spread while hot, which would have suited timbers that shift with the waves.

The sticky coatings also trapped tiny pollen grains that survived for thousands of years. The pollen came from a mix of landscapes, including coastal forests of holly oak and pine, shrubland, riverside plants, and mountain trees such as fir and beech. The pattern of coatings suggests the ship got four or five separate batches. The stern and middle shared one, while the bow had three different ones. Earlier work on the ship's ballast pointed to Brundisium, now Brindisi, as its likely birthplace. The pollen suggests some coatings were applied near there and others along the northeastern Adriatic coast, close to where the ship sank.
science.bigPicture: Archaeologists have mostly studied the wooden parts of ancient ships, and the materials that kept them watertight have received much less attention. This study suggests that pollen and chemical analysis could help trace where a vessel was built, repaired and sailed. Similar methods might one day be applied to other wrecks to compare shipbuilding traditions across the Adriatic and beyond. That could add detail to our picture of ancient sea travel that the wood alone cannot provide.
science.originalTitle: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

science.headline: Newly found viruses hint at how viruses and cell compartments evolved together
summary: Researchers at the University of Miami have identified a previously unknown group of viruses. These viruses may help fill a gap in the evolutionary story of encapsulins, which are tiny protein compartments found inside cells. The work was published in Nature Communications. Scientists had long thought encapsulins evolved from viruses, but the new evidence points to a more tangled history in which the two may have evolved from each other repeatedly over millions of years.

Both viruses and encapsulins use proteins with a particular three-dimensional shape called the HK97-fold, which can assemble into protective shells. The new viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses with these shells. They also show traits of both viruses and encapsulins, so they could be evolutionary in-between forms. The team did not grow the viruses in a lab. Instead, they searched huge genetic databases holding billions of DNA sequences from soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut and other places. They used AI tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, along with bioinformatics and models of protein behavior.
science.bigPicture: The findings suggest that the shells of viruses might sometimes do more than carry and protect genetic material. They could possibly also support chemical reactions, though the researchers say more work is needed to confirm this. If so, scientists may need to pay more attention to the non-infective forms of viruses. The search methods could also be used to study other poorly understood viruses, and the researchers say they might help in understanding newly emerging viruses and pathogens. The work may also offer clues about how early life developed, since life involves both enclosing chemical reactions and storing information that can be inherited.
science.originalTitle: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

science.headline: Researcher argues Iron Age ruler Verica, linked to Rome's invasion of Britain, was a woman
summary: Dr. Miles Russell of Bournemouth University argues that Verica, an Iron Age British ruler long assumed to be male, was a woman. Verica ruled the Atrebates, a tribe whose lands covered much of present-day Hampshire and West Sussex. Around AD 40, Verica was forced from power and fled to Rome to ask Emperor Claudius for help. The Roman historian Cassius Dio said this appeal was why Claudius chose to invade Britain in AD 43.

Russell offers several clues. The name ends in "a," as did the names of other female rulers of the era, such as Cartimandua and Boudica. Coins from Verica's reign carry the Latin title "rex," usually translated as "king," but Russell says it was not limited to men and notes that Cleopatra held it too. The coins also show a slender, feminine figure on horseback, unlike the male warriors on other British rulers' coins. Russell suggests that earlier historians assumed Verica was male because of 19th-century attitudes.
science.bigPicture: If Russell's interpretation holds, it could change how Verica is remembered, as an early and significant female leader whose exile may have set the Roman invasion in motion. He also argues that Verica was a useful ally who gave Rome tactical information, rather than merely someone who whispered in an emperor's ear. The work builds on earlier Bournemouth research suggesting women held a central place in Iron Age British society. Together, these studies may encourage researchers to look again at the role women played in the politics of the time.
science.originalTitle: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman

science.headline: Colbert-Named Trapdoor Spider Has a Genome Much Larger Than Ours
summary: A small trapdoor spider from California's coastal dunes, Aptostichus stephencolberti, has a genome about 50% larger than the human genome, even though the spider is only about the size of a quarter. Its genome has 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, compared with 46 in human cells. Researchers at UC Davis say this is the first genome sequenced from a spider in this family, and the results appeared in the Journal of Heredity.

A bigger genome does not necessarily mean more genes. About 77% of this spider's genome is repetitive DNA that shows up many times. The team also noted that spiders lack the usual repeating DNA sequences found in telomeres, the protective caps on chromosome ends. This may help explain why spider chromosomes seem to evolve faster than those of vertebrates. The spider got its name after Stephen Colbert learned in 2008 that researcher Jason Bond had named a spider after Neil Young, and Colbert asked for one of his own on his show.
science.bigPicture: The genome work is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, which aims to build genetic information that can guide conservation choices. This spider lives only along a limited stretch of Central California coast and rarely travels far from its burrow, so the data could help researchers identify separate populations that may need special protection. Rising sea levels and invasive species are listed as threats, and the team wants to learn how climate change, fire and urbanization affect genetic diversity. Understanding spider genetics might also help scientists explore spider venom compounds, some of which have shown promise as possible painkillers or as tools for controlling agricultural pests.
science.originalTitle: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s

science.headline: Why DNA's thymine may have helped early life withstand harsh sunlight
summary: Researchers at Texas A&M University have studied a long-standing puzzle in the history of life. DNA uses a building block called thymine, while RNA uses uracil instead. Thymine is more prone to certain kinds of damage from ultraviolet (UV) light, so its adoption has looked like a disadvantage, especially before Earth had a protective ozone layer.

The team, led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar, exposed thymine and uracil to controlled UV radiation meant to mimic early Earth. They then examined the molecules using light-based methods, including absorption, fluorescence and Raman spectroscopy. Their results, published in PNAS, suggest thymine tends to steer UV damage toward forms that are easier to reverse.
science.bigPicture: The findings offer a possible explanation for why thymine became part of DNA despite its apparent weakness, and they hint that managing damage may have mattered as much as resisting it for early life. The team also produced reference measurements of how these molecules respond to light, which could eventually help with detecting harmful microorganisms and checking whether UV disinfection, such as in water treatment, has worked. The researchers next hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed entirely on Earth or were partly delivered by meteorites. These remain open questions and possible directions rather than settled results.
science.originalTitle: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

medical.headline: Experimental drug PHI-101 targets resistant FLT3 leukemia in early lab and animal studies
summary: Researchers at Johns Hopkins report that an experimental drug called PHI-101 may help with a hard-to-treat form of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) known as FLT3-positive AML. Changes in the FLT3 gene occur in about one-third of people with AML. Existing FLT3-blocking drugs have helped, but some patients develop extra mutations that let the cancer escape them. The findings were published Oct. 12 in the journal Leukemia.

The team focused on a resistance mutation called F691L, sometimes described as a "gatekeeper" mutation. In lab tests, PHI-101 worked better than two FDA-approved drugs, gilteritinib and quizartinib, against cells with this change, and it had little effect on other cells. In mice with the F691L mutation, median survival was 44.4 days with PHI-101, compared with 21.4 days with gilteritinib and 19.4 days with no treatment. In another mouse experiment using human AML cells with a FLT3 mutation, median survival was 191 days with PHI-101, 133 days with gilteritinib and 108 days untreated.
medical.bigPicture: Resistance to treatment is a major limit for people with FLT3-positive AML, so a drug that still works against resistant cells could eventually add a useful option. These results come from lab and animal studies, and human trials are still at an early stage, so it is too soon to know how well the drug will work for patients. The researchers are also interested in whether PHI-101 could be used earlier in treatment or combined with other drugs, which might help improve responses and possibly prevent resistance from developing.
medical.originalTitle: Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia

medical.headline: Large UK Trial Finds Robotic Knee Replacement Matches Standard Surgery After One Year
summary: A large UK trial called RACER-Knee compared robot-assisted knee replacement with conventional surgery. The robotic system helped surgeons work with greater precision. Even so, patients in both groups reported similar pain, mobility and recovery twelve months after their operations. The results were published in The Lancet.

The study included 339 patients treated by 33 surgeons at 10 hospitals. The main measure was the Forgotten Joint Score, which shows how aware people are of their artificial joint in daily life, and the two groups scored about the same. Robotic surgery was not linked to a higher risk of serious adverse events. It took about 10.5 minutes longer and cost roughly £950 more per procedure. By current NHS spending thresholds, it was not considered cost-effective in the first year.
medical.bigPicture: Robotic systems are already used in a share of knee replacements around the world, so clear evidence about how patients fare is useful for families weighing their options and for health services deciding where to spend money. The researchers suggest the technology could become more valuable if surgeons learn the ideal placement of a knee joint for each patient and use the robot's precision to tailor the operation. They also plan to follow participants for ten years, which may show whether robotic assistance reduces the need for further knee surgery. These are possibilities, and the long-term findings will show whether any benefit appears.
medical.originalTitle: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

medical.headline: Fewer older adults with cognitive disorders take risky medications, but one in three still do
summary: A University at Buffalo study looked at 2,796 independently living adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders. It found that the share taking potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022. The researchers used the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a list of about 100 medications that may be risky for older adults, and focused on those that could be especially harmful with cognitive disorders. The data came from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey and represent about 29.7 million older Americans.

The study did not look at why exposure dropped, though the lead author points to growing awareness among clinicians and researchers. He stresses that roughly one-third of this group is still exposed. The team says medication reviews at routine appointments could help, along with tools such as the Drug Burden Index. They also describe 'deprescribing,' which means lowering a dose, stopping a drug, or switching to a milder option under medical supervision.
medical.bigPicture: Older adults now outnumber children under age 5 worldwide, and many people over 65 have at least two chronic conditions, so medication safety is likely to matter to more families. Because most of these patients have a regular source of care, the researchers say risky prescriptions could be spotted and addressed with their care team. It is not yet known whether better medication use will improve quality of life or reduce hospital and emergency room visits, so more research is needed. Anyone concerned about a medication should talk with a doctor or pharmacist before changing it.
medical.originalTitle: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

medical.headline: FDA approves giredestrant, first new early-stage breast cancer hormone therapy in over 20 years
summary: The FDA has approved giredestrant, a once-daily pill for early-stage breast cancer. It is the first new hormone therapy for this stage of the disease in more than two decades. The approval covers estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) cancer, which accounts for about 70% of all breast cancer diagnoses. The drug targets and breaks down estrogen receptors in breast tissue, cutting off the hormone that remaining cancer cells need to grow.

After surgery, patients usually take daily hormone-blocking pills for up to 10 years to help keep the cancer from returning. The article notes that the side effects of standard treatments are often harsh, and many women stop taking them early, which raises their risk of relapse. In the lidERA trial, reported in the Journal of Clinical Oncology, giredestrant improved disease-free survival and lowered the risk of cancer spreading to other organs. It was also better tolerated than standard therapy, and the benefits were seen in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women. Two oncologists quoted in the article described the approval as practice-changing.
medical.bigPicture: Hormone therapy only works if people can keep taking it, so a treatment that is easier to tolerate could matter a great deal to patients and their care teams. If giredestrant proves as effective and manageable in everyday use as it did in the trial, more women might stay on treatment for the full course, which could lower the chance of the cancer coming back. The approval may also change what doctors consider standard care for early-stage ER+ breast cancer. Individual patients would still need to talk with their own doctors about which option suits them.
medical.originalTitle: Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years

medical.headline: Gut antibody IgA may help guard against colon cancer in mice, study finds
summary: Researchers at Rockefeller University report that immunoglobulin A (IgA), an antibody found in large amounts in the digestive tract, may help protect against colon cancer. In a study published in Nature, mice that could not make IgA developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal levels. The pattern held across several different mouse models of colon cancer, which the team described as a convincing effect.

The scientists also looked at how this protection might work. Cells lining the intestine constantly divide to replace old or damaged ones, and IgA appears to keep that process in check. It binds to a receptor on those cells called DMBT1. When bacteria are present, DMBT1 sends signals that encourage cells to divide, and IgA acts like a brake on that activity. Without IgA, cells divided faster than they should, and changes in gene activity linked to cell growth showed up before any tumors could be seen.
medical.bigPicture: People with IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 people in the U.S., are known to face a higher risk of colorectal cancer, and this work may help explain why. The findings also add to our understanding of how gut bacteria, immune defenses and intestinal cells interact, possibly even in people whose immune systems are otherwise healthy. The results come from mice, so it is not yet known whether the same approach would work in people. Still, the senior author raises the possibility of stepping in before tumors form, rather than only treating cancers that already exist.
medical.originalTitle: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

medical.headline: FDA approves two-drug combination for advanced GIST after imatinib stops working
summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved bezuclastinib, taken together with sunitinib, as a second-line treatment for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). It is meant for people who have already been treated with imatinib. The decision rests on the phase 3 PEAK study, which was led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

PEAK enrolled 413 patients with advanced GIST who had previously received imatinib. They were randomly assigned to receive either the two-drug combination or sunitinib alone. The combination cut the risk of the cancer progressing or of death by 50%, and the share of patients whose tumors responded rose from 26% to 46%. Patients tolerated the combination well. One of the study's experts said it replaces sunitinib alone, which has been the standard for about 20 years.
medical.bigPicture: GIST is diagnosed in roughly 4,000 to 5,000 people in the U.S. each year, and drugs that block the KIT gene mutation have helped many of them. Tumors often become resistant, usually by picking up additional KIT mutations. Bezuclastinib targets common mutations of this kind, and the PEAK results support the idea that blocking a wider range of KIT mutations can lead to better and longer-lasting results than a single drug. This could mean more options for people whose first treatment stops working, though the material does not say how patients will fare over the long term.
medical.originalTitle: FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib as new second-line therapy for patients with GIST

medical.headline: Experimental nose drops improve memory in aging and Alzheimer's-model mice, early study finds
summary: Researchers at the University of Sydney have developed experimental nose drops that improved learning and memory in older mice. The treated animals performed about as well as young mice on tests of working memory, spatial memory and object recognition. Untreated older mice showed the usual age-related decline. The study was published in Advanced Science and led by Professor Greg Neely.

The drops deliver mRNA, a set of genetic instructions, inside tiny fat-based particles. The mRNA tells cells to make brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a natural protein that helps neurons survive and form connections. BDNF levels tend to fall with age and are linked to Alzheimer's disease. The approach builds on the same kind of mRNA technology used in COVID-19 vaccines.
medical.bigPicture: Getting medicines into the brain is difficult because the blood-brain barrier blocks many drugs. The nose may offer a non-invasive route around it, though this has so far been shown only in mice. If the results hold up in people, the approach might one day be used alongside treatments that clear amyloid plaques. It could also be explored for other conditions such as stroke or traumatic brain injury. Professor Neely said human clinical trials would be the next step, and the work is described as a proof of concept.
medical.originalTitle: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

medical.headline: FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to Nelkarmi for Previously Treated ALK-Positive Lung Cancer
summary: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has given accelerated approval to Nelkarmi (neladalkib), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with a specific kind of lung cancer. It is meant for people whose non-small cell lung cancer is ALK-positive and either locally advanced or metastatic, and who have already received treatment. The approval went to the companies Nuvalent and GSK. It covers patients who have previously taken alectinib as their only ALK inhibitor, or who have taken two or more ALK inhibitors along with platinum-based chemotherapy.

The decision rests on the Phase I/II ALKOVE-1 trial, which had 700 participants, with 222 patients in the main efficacy analysis. Among those treated only with alectinib before, 49% (33 of 67) had a confirmed response, and 52% of responders kept that response for at least 12 months. Among those who had two or more ALK inhibitors plus chemotherapy, 32% (50 of 155) responded, and 51% of responders held their response for at least 12 months. Common side effects, each affecting at least 20% of patients, included liver toxicity, musculoskeletal pain, constipation, altered taste, nerve problems in the hands and feet, swelling and fatigue. Five percent of patients stopped treatment permanently because of side effects, most often liver problems.
medical.bigPicture: People with ALK-positive lung cancer often move through several treatments over time, so having another option after earlier therapies matters. A representative of the patient group ALK Positive described the approval as important progress, noting that patients need treatments that control disease for a long time while still being tolerable. Because this is an accelerated approval, more evidence may be needed to learn how well the drug works over the long run. Families facing this diagnosis may want to talk with their care team about whether this therapy could suit their situation.
medical.originalTitle: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer

medical.headline: Study in mice explains how an experimental antibody reversed type 1 diabetes
summary: Researchers at UC Davis Health have worked out how an experimental antibody reverses type 1 diabetes in mice. In this condition, the immune system mistakenly attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, and people end up needing lifelong insulin. Most experimental treatments target T cells, but this team looked instead at the innate immune system, a less-studied part of the picture. Their results appear in the journal Diabetes.

Using a mouse model and single-cell sequencing, the team found that the antibody led to the creation of myeloid-derived suppressor cells, which help control inflammation. These cells moved to the pancreatic islet and dampened the immune activity that harms beta cells. The treatment relied on an anti-inflammatory molecule called interleukin-10; without it, these cells did not develop and the therapy stopped working. Soon after treatment, signs of stress inside beta cells also dropped sharply, which the researchers think may help restore normal blood sugar and protect beta-cell function.
medical.bigPicture: Most people are diagnosed with type 1 diabetes after damage to their beta cells has already happened, so treatments that can reverse the disease process are of real interest. Current treatments manage the condition but do not reverse the underlying autoimmune process. These findings point to immune pathways that might one day be targeted in people, though so far the work has only been done in mice and more research is needed before human studies can begin. The researchers also suggest that understanding these immune cells could possibly help with other autoimmune diseases, and future work will look at adapting the approach for people and whether similar mechanisms can be safely activated.
medical.originalTitle: How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice

medical.headline: Cannabis users tend to develop psychosis earlier, and the gap widens with age
summary: A large analysis from UNSW Sydney, published in Biological Psychiatry, found that people who use cannabis have their first episode of psychosis about two and a half years earlier, on average, than people who do not. The researchers pooled 149 studies with more than 71,000 participants. Most of the studies were done since 2011 in Europe, North America and Australia, and most focused on people diagnosed with schizophrenia.

The gap grew with age. In studies where psychosis began at an average age of 20 to 24, users were affected about 1.6 years sooner. For ages 25 to 29 the gap was 4.43 years, and for onset at 30 or later it was 6.3 years. The analysis did not find a statistically significant difference among teenagers, but the researchers said this does not mean teens are safe. Psychosis rarely starts before the mid-teens, so there is little room for onset to move earlier, and other risk factors may hide any cannabis effect.
medical.bigPicture: The study relied on existing observational research, so it cannot prove that cannabis causes psychosis or brings it on sooner. Even so, the authors say the consistent pattern, especially the large gap in older adults who may have used cannabis for longer, supports a possible causal role. They suggest it may be worth widening health warnings beyond adolescents, since the idea that waiting until the mid-20s is enough may not hold up. Because psychosis can disrupt study, work and relationships, the researchers say delaying it even by a few years could possibly help people reach those milestones and might also ease pressure on healthcare systems.
medical.originalTitle: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

medical.headline: Researchers identify 'circadian depression,' a subtype tied to the body clock that SSRIs may not help
summary: Researchers at the University of Sydney have described what they believe is a new subtype of depression, which they call circadian depression. It appears to be closely linked to the body's 24-hour internal clock, which helps control when we feel awake and when we feel sleepy. The team looked at clinical and genetic information from more than 10,000 Australians with depression. They found that nearly one in four of them, 2,604 people, showed signs of this subtype. The study focused on people with severe, recurrent or persistent depression, and the results were published in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

People with this subtype were more likely to be night owls, to sleep longer when depressed, and to wake up exhausted even after more time in bed. Their depression often began earlier in life, their symptoms tended to be more severe, and their genetic data showed a higher predisposition to inflammatory and cardiovascular problems and to neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD. The researchers also found that common antidepressants such as SSRIs and SNRIs tended to work less well for them and caused more side effects. Treatments aimed at the body clock, including light therapy, melatonin and antidepressants that target melatonin pathways, may be more suitable. The researchers advise anyone whose antidepressants are not working to talk with their clinician about their own situation.
medical.bigPicture: Depression is not one uniform illness, and this work adds to the evidence that different biological mechanisms can lie behind similar symptoms. If the findings hold up, doctors may be able to recognize this subtype sooner and offer treatments better matched to it, rather than starting everyone on the same medication. The researchers say this could be especially helpful for young people, who might otherwise spend valuable time on treatments that suit them less well. The study describes a pattern in a group of people, so it does not mean anyone should change their treatment without medical advice.
medical.originalTitle: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

medical.headline: Rising Tau Protein Linked to Worsening Depression in Older Adults With Normal Memory
summary: Scientists have found a link between a protein tied to Alzheimer's disease and growing depressive symptoms in older adults. The protein, called tau, builds up in the brain, and researchers tracked it using several brain scans. Participants also filled out questionnaires about their mood at different points during the study. The data came from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, which follows brain health over time.

Among people whose memory and thinking were still normal, faster tau buildup went along with a faster rise in depressive symptoms. Higher tau levels also helped predict more severe symptoms. The same pattern did not appear in people who already had mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease. The study, led by Teodora Markova of Brandeis University, was published in JNeurosci.
medical.bigPicture: Mood changes in later life may reflect what is happening in the brain before memory problems show up. In the future, tracking depressive symptoms over time, along with other assessments, could possibly help identify older adults at higher risk of neurodegenerative disease. The researchers stress that more work is needed to know whether early mood changes can reliably predict later cognitive decline. They plan to follow people over longer periods to see how tau, mood, and later outcomes fit together.
medical.originalTitle: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease

medical.headline: Study finds acute myeloid leukemia can start taking shape decades before diagnosis
summary: Researchers from the University of Cambridge and University College London have reconstructed how acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, develops over a lifetime. Their study, published in Nature, found that in two-thirds of the cases examined, the first cancer-driving mutation likely arose before the person turned 20. The disease can therefore be building for more than 50 years before it is diagnosed.

The team used stored yearly blood samples from a large ovarian cancer screening trial. They studied 47 women who later developed AML, whose average age at diagnosis was 72, and compared them with 46 similar women who stayed free of blood cancer. Using sensitive DNA sequencing and mathematical models, they worked backward to estimate when mutations appeared and how fast the affected cells grew.
medical.bigPicture: AML often seems to appear with little warning, and survival is poor: only about one in six patients lives at least five years after diagnosis. If growth rates can be measured from a few blood samples, doctors might one day be able to estimate who is at greatest risk years ahead of time. The researchers also suggest that slowing the growth of a high-risk clone over a decade or more could lower the chance it becomes leukemia, though this is still a possibility rather than a proven treatment. Most people with these blood-cell mutations never develop AML, so better ways to tell who is at risk could matter a great deal.
medical.originalTitle: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

medical.headline: U.S. Loses Measles Elimination Status as Survey Finds Widespread Confusion About Vaccines
summary: The Pan American Health Organization confirmed on Nov. 17, 2026, that the United States no longer qualifies as having eliminated measles. The country first earned that status in 2000, which meant no strain of the virus had spread continuously for 12 months or longer. The change comes during the nation's worst measles resurgence in decades. The CDC counted 5,412 confirmed cases in 2026 as of Nov. 12, more than double the 2,290 reported in all of 2025.

A new Annenberg Public Policy Center survey of 1,028 U.S. adults, taken Nov. 6-8, 2026, found many people are unsure about measles and its vaccine. About 64% correctly rejected the claim that childhood vaccines cause autism, while 17% believed it and 19% did not know. Research has found no evidence of a link, and the World Health Organization's vaccine safety committee reaffirmed this in 2025. Only 9% knew that about 1 in 1,000 infected children die from measles, and just 34% knew two vaccine doses are recommended. The CDC says one dose gives 93% protection and two doses give 97%.
medical.bigPicture: Losing elimination status shows how falling vaccination rates can have national consequences, according to the survey's lead researcher, Kathleen Hall Jamieson. Earlier Annenberg research found that people who accept false vaccine claims are less likely to recommend the MMR vaccine to others, so confusion may influence real decisions. Clearer public information about the risks of measles and the recommended two-dose schedule could help families make informed choices. Whether case numbers fall and the status is regained will depend on future vaccination levels and how the disease spreads.
medical.originalTitle: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist

technology.headline: New Rubberlike Semiconductor Stretches and Springs Back While Conducting Electricity Well
summary: Researchers have developed a polymer semiconductor that can stretch like rubber and return to its original shape. The work was led by Professor Joon Hak Oh at Seoul National University, with teams from Queensland University of Technology in Australia and Fudan University in China. It is an n-type material, a kind of semiconductor that uses electrons to carry charge. Stretchable n-type materials have so far performed far worse electrically than their p-type counterparts.

The team added about 10% of a poorly soluble molecular structure, once seen as a drawback, to an n-type polymer with strong electrical performance. These molecules stack together and act as "nano-anchors" that hold the soft polymer chains in place, helping them return to their original arrangement after stretching while keeping paths open for electricity. In tests, a conventional n-type polymer cracked after a single stretch to 1.75 times its length. The new material showed no cracking after 1,000 cycles of stretching to twice its length and releasing.
technology.bigPicture: Electronics that bend and stretch with the body need materials that can survive repeated movement without losing performance. Because stretchable n-type semiconductors have lagged behind p-type ones, this result may help close that gap. The researchers expect the technology could eventually be used in wearable health devices that move with the skin while measuring signals such as pulse and blood oxygen levels. It could also be used in wearable displays and electronic skin for robots, though these remain possible future uses rather than finished products.
technology.originalTitle: Rubberlike semiconductor combines elasticity and high electrical performance for stretchable electronics

technology.headline: Experimental bionic hand lets a user feel pressure, and he's testing it at home
summary: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. He now uses an experimental prosthetic that is wired to nerves in his forearm and lets him sense pressure. He says he can handle delicate things such as grapes, eggs and a loved one's hand. He is the ninth person in a University of Utah clinical trial to have the device implanted, and the first to take it home and use it on his own.

The hand is part of the LUKE arm, which was approved by the FDA in 2014. The trial focuses less on the arm itself and more on a new way of linking it to the nervous system, so users can control movement and get feedback about pressure. Surgeons placed electrode arrays in three nerves in his arm and added 24 electrodes in nearby muscles. A computer system was then trained to turn nerve signals into hand and wrist movements. Teaching it to produce sensations took much longer, about three days according to the lab director.
technology.bigPicture: Researchers want to learn how useful this kind of hand really is in daily life, when it helps, and where it falls short. They also want to see how it affects Davidson's well-being, brain and nervous system. What they find could help shape future prosthetics that offer both movement and a sense of touch. Because this is an early trial with a small number of participants, it is too soon to say how widely such devices might be used.
technology.originalTitle: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

technology.headline: EU Unveils Quantum Act, Hoping to Avoid Repeating Its Mistakes on AI
summary: The European Union is set to present plans on Wednesday that it says will turn the continent into a global leader in quantum computing. Officials worry Europe could fall behind again, since it already trails the United States and China in artificial intelligence. Quantum computing uses the physics of atoms and subatomic particles to solve certain problems much faster than ordinary computers. The EU says it wants to be a world leader in the field by 2030.

A draft of the proposed law, called the Quantum Act, was seen by AFP and could still change. It would give European companies priority for public money over firms from outside the EU, though public bodies could also buy from countries the EU has partnerships with. Tech chief Henna Virkkunen is due to present it in the European Parliament, and it will only become law after talks between EU states and Parliament. An EU official said the aim is to avoid making the same mistakes as with AI, by investing early and helping companies grow larger.
technology.bigPicture: Europe is already strong in quantum research but lags in turning it into commercial products, so this law is an attempt to close that gap. The EU points to possible benefits such as new drugs, earlier medical diagnoses, longer-lasting batteries and secure communications, and quantum might even speed up AI. There are also risks, since quantum technology could break the encryption that protects digital data. One industry voice said quantum could become the next AI, develop alongside it, or fail to gain enough uptake, depending on the rules, funding and government choices.
technology.originalTitle: After AI, EU bets on quantum as next big thing

technology.headline: Researchers Send a One-Word Message Through a Wall Using Changes in Gravity
summary: Researchers at the University of Queensland have shown that information can be sent through a solid wall using gravity instead of radio waves. In the university's Parnell Building, they repeatedly moved an old elevator between two floors. This shifted its 1.8-metric-ton counterweight between two positions, and each position stood for a 0 or a 1.

On the other side of a brick wall, a very sensitive instrument called a gravimeter sat in a bathroom. It picked up the tiny changes in gravitational pull caused by the moving counterweight. By decoding those readings, the team recovered the word "Gravity." The idea grew out of earlier work on a contactless weighbridge, which aims to find the weight of trucks by measuring their tiny gravitational pull.
technology.bigPicture: Ordinary materials can weaken or block radio and Wi-Fi signals, but they do not screen out gravitational fields. That is why this approach is of interest, even though the researchers describe the current system as far from practical. Speed would depend on the size of the mass, how fast it can be moved, and how sensitive the detector is. If better sensors were developed, gravity-based messaging might one day be useful where conventional signals cannot get through, but that remains a possibility rather than a certainty.
technology.originalTitle: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

technology.headline: Salt-Based Air Conditioner Cuts Energy Use 40% in Georgia Waffle House Test
summary: In July 2025, technicians installed a new kind of air conditioner at a Waffle House in Macon, Georgia, where outdoor temperatures were around 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius). The system was co-invented by researchers at the National Laboratory of the Rockies and a startup called Blue Frontier. It was the first real-world pilot of the design. According to the article, the kitchen cooks noticed the difference within minutes and said it was the first time they weren't sweating in the middle of summer.

The pilot used 40% less energy than the building's earlier air conditioner and cut operating costs by 65%. Power use during peak grid hours, when electricity costs the most, dropped by 89%. The system uses a salt-based liquid to pull moisture from the air, then cools the dried air through evaporative cooling. Because dehumidifying takes up more than half of an air conditioner's energy, handling it separately is a big part of the savings. The system can also be recharged, like a battery, by restoring its salt solution at times when electricity is cheap.
technology.bigPicture: Air conditioning often creates the highest peaks of electricity demand, which can strain power grids. A system that uses less power overall and shifts when it draws electricity could, in theory, help ease that strain and lower costs for the businesses that run it. This was a single pilot at one restaurant, so it is not yet clear how the results would hold up in other buildings or climates. If the approach does scale, it could become one way to keep spaces comfortable during hot weather while reducing pressure on the grid.
technology.originalTitle: Georgia Waffle House cuts cooling energy use by 40% with new salt-based AC system

technology.headline: Space lasers send data fast, but clouds make them less reliable than radio
summary: Spacecraft have talked to Earth by radio since Sputnik, but crowded and tightly regulated radio frequencies make it hard to expand capacity. Infrared lasers can carry far more data. A NASA demonstration called TBIRD sent 200 gigabits per second from orbit and moved five terabytes in one five-minute pass, though it had near-perfect conditions.

A paper by Dr. Slava Turyshev argues that reliability, not speed, is the main problem. A laser beam from low Earth orbit may cover a patch under 20 meters across, so keeping it aimed at a telescope is hard. Ground stations must also switch off uplink lasers when planes pass overhead. Turbulent air distorts the light, and thick clouds block it completely.
technology.bigPicture: The paper suggests that sharing ground stations among several satellite companies could make the costs more reasonable, especially if the stations stay busy at least half the time. Common standards from CCSDS and the U.S. Space Development Agency aim to let equipment from different suppliers work together. Turyshev sees little chance that lasers will replace radio soon. A hybrid setup could use lasers for large video and imagery downloads and radio for steering and emergencies, which might help keep astronauts and space systems connected in any weather.
technology.originalTitle: Space lasers are fast, but clouds still rule the forecast

technology.headline: Korean Team's Thin Lens Brings Clearer Daytime Images to AR Glasses
summary: Augmented reality (AR) glasses place information such as directions or text over the scene in front of the wearer. A research team led by Professor Junsuk Rho of POSTECH, working with Samsung Research, has developed a way to cut down on wasted light inside the thin lens of such glasses. Much of the dimming in current designs comes from light escaping in unintended directions. Because the wasted light is reduced, the images stay brighter, even when the wearer's eye moves.

The team studied the whole path that light takes through the lens and designed it with great precision at a tiny scale. To handle color, they stacked one layer that mainly passes blue and green light on top of another that mainly passes red and green. This helped even out how efficiently each color reaches the eye. The finished waveguide is 1.5 mm thick. In prototype glasses, it showed white text over real outdoor scenery in bright conditions and color images indoors. The images stayed visible when the eye shifted within a certain range.
technology.bigPicture: For AR glasses to work in daily life, they need to be thin and light like ordinary eyeglasses and still show clear images in bright places. This research suggests that using light more efficiently could help with both goals. The researchers expect the approach could lead to everyday glasses that show directions or work information, and it might also lower power use while keeping the screen bright. Several technical problems remain, so how soon such glasses could appear is still unknown.
technology.originalTitle: Thin lenses, clear images in bright daylight: A step toward everyday AR glasses

technology.headline: Rewritable display built on antimony selenide can hold an image for months without power
summary: Researchers at the ARC Centre of Excellence for Transformative Meta-Optical Systems (TMOS) report a reflective display, made with a material called antimony selenide, that can keep an image on screen for months without being powered. Phones, laptops and televisions need a constant supply of power to keep showing a picture. The team, from RMIT and the Australian National University, says its approach could lead to much lower energy use. In one test, an image of a koala was left for three months in ordinary conditions with no noticeable change.

The material is a phase-change material, meaning its atoms can be rearranged again and again between an irregular (amorphous) state and an orderly (crystalline) one. To erase the screen, the researchers heated it evenly to about 200°C, which resets it to a blank image. To draw, they used short laser pulses that cool quickly and lock the atoms into the irregular state, creating different colored regions. A map of Australia, the TMOS logo and a koala were drawn and erased, and no leftover image was visible even under a 5× microscope. So far the colors range from deep blues through grays to oranges, which lead researcher Dr. Phuong Yen Le describes as a limited range.
technology.bigPicture: If this approach can be developed further, it might lead to displays that use very little energy because they only need power when the image changes. Two big steps remain, according to Le: the current version relies on a laser, and it would need to become a fully electronic device. The color range would also need to widen, which may require changing the device's structure. Whether it can become a commercial product is still an open question.
technology.originalTitle: New rewritable displays can show an image for months without power

technology.headline: IBM and University of Chicago Quantum Computer Completes Hard Task With Verified Results
summary: Researchers at IBM and the University of Chicago report that an IBM quantum computer finished an extremely complex calculation in about 15 minutes. They say the leading ways of simulating that calculation on conventional computers would take impractically long. The team also found a way to build statistical confidence that the quantum computer's answers were accurate, which has been one of the field's biggest obstacles.

The team describes the result as meeting the basic criteria for quantum advantage: doing a task beyond the practical reach of classical methods while producing results that can be trusted. To get there, they designed a more structured version of a common benchmark called random circuit sampling. This structure lets errors be detected during the computation. The experiment used 70 protected logical qubits, 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical T gates. Encoding the circuits gave logical error rates 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates. The researchers have made their circuits and results publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.
technology.bigPicture: The experiment was meant to demonstrate quantum advantage, not to solve an everyday real-world problem. Even so, it tackles two things needed for large-scale quantum computing: keeping errors under control and knowing whether the answers can be trusted. If these methods continue to work as machines grow, quantum computers could one day help with scientific and industrial problems that are currently out of reach. That remains a possibility, and the researchers describe this result as a step in that direction.
technology.originalTitle: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes

technology.headline: Lab-built 'active' materials can crawl, walk and dig using their own internal energy
summary: Most everyday materials, like metal, glass, concrete and rubber, only change shape when something outside pushes or pulls on them. Researchers from the universities of Amsterdam, New South Wales and Cambridge have been building a different kind of material, called active matter, which carries its own source of energy. They made it from simple parts such as small motors, rods and rubber bands, and their work has led to two recently accepted scientific papers.

In the first study, the team linked rods into a flexible chain and placed small motors at the joints. The motors made the links uneven, so moving one rod affected its neighbor differently than the reverse. Where an ordinary material would bend and snap just once, these chains could buckle and snap again and again. That repeated motion can look like crawling, walking or even digging. The work appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
technology.bigPicture: These findings suggest that how parts are connected can matter as much as how strong or active each part is. The researchers say the chain results point toward materials that could do several jobs on their own, and that could be useful in soft robots whose bodies produce complex movements without a central control system. They also believe the second finding could help in understanding and designing systems made of tiny active structures, such as biological gels, sheets of closely connected cells and networks that mimic aspects of biological information processing. These are possibilities, and the work so far is based on laboratory structures built from simple parts.
technology.originalTitle: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures

technology.headline: Laser 'printing' of steel could help repair aging bridges instead of replacing them
summary: The U.K. has about 300 million metric tons of iron and steel in its buildings and transport infrastructure, and many structures are older than people realize. A report from the Royal Academy of Engineering warned that action is urgent. Repairs and replacements need more steel, and making or recycling steel carries a climate cost, even with lower-carbon methods.

One option is additive manufacturing, which builds objects layer by layer. In a method called wire-fed laser-directed energy deposition, a thin metal wire is fed into a laser beam. The beam melts the wire and a small patch of the old steel, so new metal bonds directly to the original and is added only where it is needed. Siemens and Fastech already offer additive manufacturing for onsite repairs of other equipment, such as steam turbine rotors.
technology.bigPicture: If repairs like this prove reliable, they could help keep older bridges and buildings in use longer. The article says that keeping just 1% of the U.K.'s steel stock in service could avoid 3 million metric tons of new steel production. It also says focused renovation can produce 84%–93% lower emissions than replacement and can let bridges stay open. Before that can happen, engineers need to learn how old and new steel behave together, so they can judge how much extra safe life a repair really adds.
technology.originalTitle: Technology for 'printing' steel could help extend the life of aging bridges and buildings

technology.headline: Rice University Team Makes Fast-Charging Battery Graphite in Just 0.2 Seconds
summary: Many lithium-ion batteries, including those in cars, phones and cameras, use graphite in one of their electrodes, called the anode. When a battery charges, lithium ions move into this graphite, and how fast they can travel through it is a key limit on charging speed. A research group led by James Tour at Rice University has now made a synthetic graphite that supports much faster charging.

The method starts with petroleum coke, a low-cost carbon leftover from oil refining, mixed with a small amount of a nickel compound. One short, powerful electrical pulse heats the mixture to about 2,500°C, and the carbon quickly arranges itself into orderly graphite layers. The whole process takes two-tenths of a second, whereas making graphite normally takes long periods of very high heat.
technology.bigPicture: Charging speed and the cost of making battery materials are both big concerns for electric vehicles, and this work tackles them together. If the approach holds up beyond the lab, it could possibly lead to batteries that charge faster and are cheaper and cleaner to produce. The researchers also found that the nickel's main job is helping build the graphite structure, since the benefits stayed even after more than 99% of the leftover nickel was removed. That finding may guide future work on making materials with less energy, though the material's real-world performance still needs to be shown.
technology.originalTitle: New synthetic graphite paves way for rapid EV charging

technology.headline: Prototype drone folds its arms to squeeze through gaps about half its width
summary: A team of researchers in Europe has built a prototype drone whose side arms fold when they touch the edges of a narrow opening. The drone shrinks from 12.3 inches (31.3 cm) wide to 5.6 inches (14.1 cm), a 55% reduction. Earlier folding drones had managed up to 29%. Unlike many past designs, it has no dedicated motors for folding, which keeps it simpler.

The team found the design using an automated search. Computer simulations tested candidate shapes and joint stiffness, including how the arms touch edges, fold, pass through an opening and recover. The best candidate at each step guided the next round. The finished drone uses 3D-printed parts and spring-loaded joints that stay rigid in normal flight but bend on contact. In flight tests it crossed a 5.9-inch (15 cm) gap at roughly 4.5 mph (2 m/s) and passed through a 15.7-inch-long tube. It also handled angled approaches to a 7.9-inch gap without problems up to 20°, though an arm slipped out of place once at 30° and several times at 35°.
technology.bigPicture: Drones are often sent into places that are hard for people to reach, and those places can include tight or oddly shaped openings. A simple passive design that folds on contact, without extra motors, could be one way to help drones fit through such spaces. The researchers suggest that more accurate simulations might lead to designs that perform even better in the real world. This is still an early prototype, though, and the rough crossings and arm slips at steeper angles show there is more work to do.
technology.originalTitle: New drone prototype folds itself through gaps half its width during flight

technology.headline: Scientists Pin Down How a Key Crystal Handles Light, Aiding Faster Optical Devices
summary: Researchers led by KAIST, working with Caltech and other partners, have measured in detail how barium titanate (BTO) guides and absorbs light. BTO is a promising material for devices that send information using light. Its optical properties have been hard to measure reliably for decades, and past reports often conflicted with one another.

The trouble comes from tiny regions inside the crystal, called domains, that point in different directions and respond to light differently. To avoid mixing these responses, the team studied two kinds of single-crystal samples with fairly consistent domain orientations. They used a technique that tracks how light's polarization changes, and they covered wavelengths from ultraviolet to far-infrared. In the 2-10 micrometer range, they found very low absorption, with an extinction coefficient of about 10 -5. The team also built a way to predict how a crystal with several domains will behave overall, based on each domain's orientation and share of the crystal.
technology.bigPicture: Engineers need dependable numbers on how a material bends and absorbs light before they can design parts that carry data with little signal loss. With these measurements, they may be able to model components on a computer before building them, which could mean fewer prototypes and redesigns. The researchers also suggest the findings could support devices that produce light at different wavelengths and photonic circuits for quantum information. These remain possibilities, and the study itself is about understanding the material rather than presenting a finished product.
technology.originalTitle: A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet

ai.headline: Anthropic CEO rejects claim he wants people to give up free will to AI
summary: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, said on Wednesday that he does not think humans should hand over their free will to AI systems. In a long post on X, he called the suggestion "absurd" and wrote that legitimacy and self-determination should never be given up for the sake of efficiency or security. The post came a week after Anthropic's record-setting stock market debut.

He was responding to an Axios article on the AI debate. Without naming anyone, he criticized "some AI CEOs" who say AI should be just a tool but do not do anything different in their products. Meta's chief AI officer Alexandr Wang and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have both recently said similar things about keeping human agency. Elon Musk reposted Amodei's statement with the single word "interesting."
ai.bigPicture: This exchange shows that leading AI companies are publicly working out how much control machines should have and how much should stay with people. Anthropic's IPO filing says each new Claude version speeds up development of the next, and that Claude wrote over 90% of the contributions to its codebase in September. That makes the question of limits on self-improving AI more concrete. If the companies spell out where those limits sit, it could shape how future products are built and how the public judges them. For now, the lines remain unspecified, so it is unclear what any limits would look like.
ai.originalTitle: Anthropic chief denies wanting humans to 'surrender' free will to AI

ai.headline: Singapore's Punggol Digital District Serves as a Real-World Testing Ground for Robots and AI
summary: In a government-built district called Punggol Digital District, Singapore is trying out technology that could become part of daily life. In a staged demonstration, AI-powered cameras and sensors spotted a coffee spill at an office block. A cleaning robot then left its dock, rode an elevator to the eighth floor and cleaned up the mess without human help.

The district covers 50 hectares and has eight businesses and office blocks, a mall, a university campus and a metro station. A central digital platform gathers data from thousands of cameras and sensors, and AI analyzes it, with human operators helping. The system can respond to problems, anticipate disruption and cut energy use and waste. For example, it can reduce elevator movements when demand is low and adjust air-conditioning in real time. Staff also use a digital replica of the district on a giant screen to spot or predict problems.
ai.bigPicture: Testing robots and connected systems across a whole district, rather than in separate places, may help companies see how the technology works in everyday settings. A Panasonic executive said similar trials in Japan took longer because he had to deal with many separate building managers, regulators and agencies. If the approach works, it could possibly help cities cope with fewer workers while keeping public spaces clean and safe. Safety rules are still being developed, and the people interviewed said they had no privacy worries, so how these tools are received more widely remains to be seen.
ai.originalTitle: Robots roam Singapore's urban AI testing ground

ai.headline: AI-made holiday ads promote products that don't exist, leaving shoppers with losses
summary: Short vertical video ads made with artificial intelligence are drawing millions of views ahead of Black Friday. They promote items such as themed Advent calendars, heated robes and pet accessories. Experts say holiday gift scams are not new, but AI has made it cheaper to produce a convincing product demonstration. In an October 2026 shopping survey, 43% of Americans said they had been fooled by ads created with the technology.

Shoppers describe a range of problems. Content creator Maggie McGaugh, who makes unboxing videos about these items, says what arrives is usually much smaller and poorer in quality than the ads suggest. One shopper, Tia Evans, paid more than $200 for four robes after seeing the ad repeatedly. The website then went dark and her messages went unanswered. Another, Michelle Richard, is still waiting for her order. H&M said its name was falsely used to promote products it does not sell. Some shoppers also reported that their card details were misused on gambling websites.
ai.bigPicture: The story shows how cheap AI tools can make a fake product look real, and how seeing an ad many times can make it feel trustworthy. Digital media expert Christina Inge describes the holiday season as a "perfect storm" for impulse buying. Shoppers may need to be more careful about unfamiliar sellers and to check payment protections before buying. Retailers whose names are misused could also face pressure to respond, though the article does not say what may happen next.
ai.originalTitle: Fake gifts, real losses as AI ads proliferate

ai.headline: Study finds AI can often identify 'anonymous' speakers from small personal details
summary: Researchers at Northeastern University, Tianshi Li and Jianing Wen, tested how well AI can work out who someone is from an interview with the obvious clues removed. They picked 822 people with known identities from Reddit's "Ask Me Anything" community and turned their backgrounds into fictional interviews about work and technology. Names and other clear giveaways were taken out. The strongest AI systems still identified the speaker in roughly 400 of the interviews, often by combining details that seem harmless alone, such as a job description, a project and the years spent on it.

Web access helped the AI, but it was not essential: three models still named 15% to 28% of speakers using only what they learned in training. When the bots reported high or very high confidence, about nine in ten answers were right. In a second test on 143 interviews with even more clues removed, the AI still identified 85.3% of speakers. Telling the AI to protect identities did not fix the problem, because its web searches surfaced pages that named the speaker, and those links could be seen in the results. The researchers then trained another AI model to flag revealing passages, and removing them cut the average success rate from 75.1% to 35.1% on the smaller test set.
ai.bigPicture: Experts quoted in the article say anonymous data has never been as simple as removing a few identifiers, but AI makes re-identification cheaper and easier for people without special skills. That could mean people who once spoke freely on message boards face a higher risk of being exposed. The same methods might also help people decide what to share or keep separate across accounts, help developers build tools that warn about risky details before something is posted, and help police trace anonymous threats or protect victims and witnesses. Research like this could also give the public stronger grounds to ask lawmakers for privacy protections.
ai.originalTitle: Think you're anonymous online? AI can blow your cover

ai.headline: Study Says Common AI Buzzwords May Mislead the Public About What the Technology Does
summary: Researchers at Simon Fraser University say the words the AI industry uses may be confusing people about how the technology works and what harm it can cause. In a study published in the journal AI and Ethics, they call this practice "glosslighting." The term combines a glossary of words with gaslighting, meaning manipulating how people understand something. The authors argue that vague, abstract language helps shape public opinion, hide harms and avoid scrutiny.

The team gives a couple of examples. Saying data lives in "the cloud" skips over the large, energy-intensive data centers and server farms that store and process it. Calling a chatbot's false output a "hallucination" makes it sound humanlike and suggests a simple slip, rather than a systemic error a company should answer for. The study was led by assistant professor Nicholas Vincent, with computing science student Ayana Hussain and Ph.D. candidate Weina Jin. Vincent says most of their suggested alternative terms would make communication easier, though some may need extra explanation.
ai.bigPicture: The researchers say more precise wording could make AI companies more transparent and accountable. It could also challenge the idea that ever more powerful AI is inevitable. Vincent suggests that as shoppers become pickier, they may ask for clearer descriptions of what an AI product actually is. If that happens, it could encourage plainer language, but the study does not say whether the industry will change how it talks.
ai.originalTitle: 'Glosslighting' the public: Study calls for overhaul of industry-led AI buzzwords

ai.headline: Study of Sierra Leone teachers suggests chatbots could be a cheaper route to information than web search
summary: Researchers studied how teachers in Sierra Leone used an AI chatbot called theTeacher.AI, which works inside WhatsApp like any other contact. More than 500 teachers were trained to use it, and over 100 of them answered a survey. The idea behind the study is that although mobile phones are common in Africa, only 37% of people there use the internet. Many of those who do go online prefer social networking apps to search engines, partly because search results lead to large foreign websites that use up costly data.
